abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Gene and cell therapies have been gaining popularity with market approvals by the US Food and Drug Administration, European Medicines Agency, and other regulatory bodies. Adeno-associated viral vector gene therapies approved for rare inherited diseases and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies approved as a novel modality for hematological anti-cancer therapies have led the way in a new paradigm of drug discovery and development. Previously incurable diseases such as hemophilia A and B have now been effectively treated via adeno-associated viral vector-mediated gene therapy, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies have provided cures for lymphomas in patients refractory to all previous treatments demonstrating the great promise of these agents. Immunogenicity is a major factor hampering the efficacy and eligible population of gene therapies as well as creates a safety risk for some individuals. Inherent attributes of adeno-associated viral vector gene and autologous chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies present a unique set of factors that can influence immunogenicity to the drug compared to widely used small-molecule or biologic drugs. This review outlines immunogenicity concerns of gene and cell therapy, and their clinical manifestations. We detail mechanisms by which these therapies can trigger innate, humoral, and cellular immunity. Additionally, we give an in-depth discussion of in silico, in vitro, and in vivo immunogenicity screening methods that have been applied in gene and cell therapy development, and the utility of each.

sec.p: Accepted 2025 Nov 2; Issue date 2026.

tr.td: In-depth discussion of the multi-faceted mechanisms of immunogenic responses to gene and cell therapies. This includes both innate and adaptive immune recognition and mediators as well as key factors of the therapeutics that interact with these mediators.
Overview of current immunogenicity prediction and monitoring methods are included: in silico, in vitro, and in vivo.

Key benefits and pitfalls for each method as well as key findings from each that has expanded our current understanding of anti-adeno-associated viral vector and anti-chimeric antigen receptor T-cell immunity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Adeno-associated viral vectors (AAVs) are naturally occurring non-pathogenic viruses that can transduce a variety of cell types in humans and other mammals. They are composed of a protein icosahedral capsid containing a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) genome. Recombinant AAV capsids have been developed to replace the wild-type ssDNA genome with a specific gene of interest, also known as a transgene, to correct monogenic disorders. Successful transduction can provide years to lifelong gene correction in individuals. Chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR T) are genetically engineered T cells from human donors that express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) targeting antigens upregulated on or unique to cancer cells. Upon CAR binding to cancer cells, CAR T become activated and secrete cytotoxic granules to eliminate the cancer. Chimeric antigen receptor T cells are currently used to treat hematological malignancies that are resistant to multiple other lines of therapy and have shown great success in the clinic.

Concerns of immunogenicity to AAV or CAR T have risen as more therapies reach clinical trials and market approvals. Immunogenicity can impact the safety and efficacy of gene and cell therapies, which has driven extensive investigations into contributing factors and mitigation strategies for AAV and CAR T immunogenicity. This review first discusses mechanisms of immunogenicity currently known, which range from innate to adaptive immune responses. Furthermore, we discuss the influence of pre-existing immunity and memory responses to AAV and CAR T therapy. Finally, we meticulously go through various immunogenicity screening tools used in the development of these therapies. This review focuses on AAV gene therapy and autologous CAR T therapy immunogenicity. Depictions of recombinant AAV, transgenic protein, and CAR constructs with respective factors influencing immunogenicity to each are shown in Fig. 1. Other gene therapies such as CRISPR-based or lentiviral-based in vivo gene therapies are outside the scope of this article. Similarly, for the CAR T discussion, we will not address T-cell receptor T cells, CAR natural killer (NK) cells, or allogeneic cell therapy.

sec.title: Innate Immunity: Acute Toxicity and Priming Adaptive Immunogenicity
sec.p: Multiple cell types and immune sensors have been implicated in the generation of anti-AAV immunity. This section aims to give an overview of our current understanding of how an anti-AAV immune response is generated, particularly the distribution and role of innate immune sensors in priming an adaptive immune response as well as other key components of innate immunity implicated in AAV immunogenicity. This includes complement system and NK cells. Additionally, the distinctions between these factors in murine and human populations are discussed.

sec.title: Toll-Like Receptors (TLRs) and Cytosolic Innate Immune Sensors
sec.p: The innate immune system is the body’s first line of defense that provides a rapid non-specific response to invading pathogens. Pattern-recognition receptors, Toll-like receptors (TLRs) 2 and 9, have been implicated in AAV immunogenicity. Toll-like receptor 2 is a receptor recognizing bacterial, fungal, and viral infections and is present on the cell surface. It is expressed in the spleen, peripheral blood leukocytes, phagocytes, eosinophils, basophils, mast cells, monocytes, myeloid dendritic cells (DCs), B cells, NK cells, and non-immune cells in the skin, respiratory, intestinal, and genitourinary tracts [1–6]. Toll-like receptor 9 is present in the endosome of cells, and is sensitive to unmethylated CpG motifs in microbial DNA. Toll-like receptor 9 has a less widespread expression throughout the body compared with TLR2. Toll-like receptor 9 is restricted to immune cell types and is present on most cell types labeled above, but is not present on myeloid DCs and has higher expression on B cells than TLR2 [6, 7]. Toll-like receptor 2 and TLR9 signal through the MyD88 adaptor protein, which causes a cascade of enzymatic processes resulting in the translocation of transcription factors nuclear factor-κB and IRF5, resulting in the production of proinflammatory cytokines [8]. Toll-like receptor 9 can also trigger IRF7 translocation to result in type I interferon (IFN) production [9].

Toll-like receptor 2 has been shown to bind to the AAV capsid upon entry into cells, while the CpG motifs contained within the inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) of the AAV ssDNA can bind TLR9 in the endosome or lysosome while entering the cell [10]. Binding these receptors induces the production of proinflammatory cytokines and can shift resulting adaptive immune responses to T helper-1 rather than T helper-2 pathways [11]. Binding to TLR9 by AAV requires genomic material normally within the capsid to be exposed to the receptor in the endosome or lysosome [12]. It is possible that some AAV can be degraded in the lysosome resulting in the release of genomic material, but through analysis of the endocytic pathway of AAVs into cells it was shown that VP1 has distinct conformation structure changes upon acidification that expose the VP1u domain to interact with the endosomal membrane to escape into the cytoplasm [13]. The conformational changes could also result in the DNA to be exposed on the surface of the AAV to interact with TLR9 [13].

Apart from TLRs, innate cytosolic sensors may also be implicated in the innate immune response to AAV. RIG-I and MDA5 are expressed in almost all mammalian cell types and typically respond to viral infections [14]. RIG-I senses 5′-triphosphorylated blunt-ended short double-stranded (dsRNA) or single-stranded RNA hairpins of positive-strand and negative-strand viruses, while MDA5, in contrast, preferentially recognizes long dsRNA and binds to the RNA backbone of dsRNA viruses or dsRNA replication intermediates of positive-strand RNA viruses [14]. Recombinant AAVs contain ssDNA flanked by two ITRs that will not bind these innate cytosolic immune sensors directly. Rather, both ITRs have promoter activity that could produce sense and anti-sense RNAs that can form dsRNA, which is recognized by both MDA5 and RIG-I. This in turn will cause the production of type I IFNs and an inflammatory microenvironment in transduced cells, which has been shown to impact stable transgene production [15]. The co-administration of AAV with a TLR7 agonist to mimic dsRNA sensing in murine models did not trigger antibody formation, but these studies did not account for possible MDA5 or RIG-I dsRNA sensing [16].

Mouse models have been instrumental in studying the implications of innate immunity and its contribution to mounting an adaptive immune response. An elegant set of studies immunizing wild-type or TLR9 knock-out (KO) mice with AAV2 containing a prominent anti-OVA CD8+ T-cell epitope inserted into its capsid helped elucidate this mechanism [17]. Two weeks after immunization, stained OT-1 cells were administered to the mice, and proliferation of cells was monitored. TLR9 KO nearly eliminated the proliferation of the adoptively transferred cells compared with wild-type mice, which showed clear connections between innate immune stimulation and resulting anti-AAV capsid adaptive immunity [17]. Apart from just implicating TLR9 in the generation of immune response, the Herzog group was able to show the process to be Myd88 dependent and delineate the response to require TLR9 sensing in plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs) to prime conventional DCs, which cross-present the capsid antigen for CD8+ T-cell activation [17]. Furthermore, in a follow-up paper, it was shown that this interaction was driven by type I IFN production by pDCs and required CD4+ T-cell help, but was not affected by knocking out NK cells [18].

This mechanism is substantiated in human data by a set of factors. First, pDCs in human blood can produce type I IFN in a TLR9-dependent manner [19]. Second, both mouse and human anti-capsid CD8+ T-cell responses are shown to be dose dependent and can be somewhat mitigated in humans via the use of corticosteroids, which may be due to the reduction of circulating pDCs [20, 21]. Last, the presence of CpG motifs in the vector genome’s ITRs results in a greater CD8+ T-cell response to the vector, which is likely due to CpG binding to TLR9 [12]. However, it is difficult to predict the cytotoxicity of CD8+ T cells in humans using mouse models. In the first hepatic gene transfer trial for hemophilia B using the AAV2-FIX vector, healthy subjects showed strong cytotoxic CD8+ T cells with declining transgene expression, but murine CD8+ T cells showed little activity against AAV-transduced cells [22].

sec.title: Natural Killer (NK) Cells and Complement
sec.p: Natural killer cells circulate and rely on a balance of activation and inhibitory signals from interacting cells to become activated. For instance, major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules on a healthy cell surface act as an inhibitory ligand, and loss of MHC I during a viral infection can shift the NK cell to an activated state to eliminate the infected cell [23]. Cell stress during a viral infection or tumor generation can cause activating surface receptors to initiate a NK cell response [23]. Apart from this, NK cells are the effector cells during antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity (ADCC). This occurs when an antibody binds a surface antigen on a cell and subsequently binds Fc receptors FcγRIIIA and/or FcγRIIC on the surface of NK cells [24]. This in turn causes degranulation of NK cells to lyse the antibody-bound cell.

Evidence is accumulating that NK cells play a role in initiating immunity against AAVs. As stated previously, CD8+ T-cell responses did not differ in NK cell KO mice versus wild-type mice. Under further investigation, seronegative healthy human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) exposed to AAV2, 5, or 8 peptide pools showed distinct IFN-γ production by NK cells 24 hours after stimulation [25]. Tumor necrosis factor-α was also increased but this increase was observed in seropositive individuals, suggesting a different NK response in naïve versus donors previously infected with AAVs [25]. Though the mechanism of NK cell activation is relatively unknown, two theories are plausible. Adeno-associated viral vectors are either endocytosed by neighboring cells, causing upregulation of NK cell activation ligands, or by downregulation of inhibitory ligands, resulting in increased NK cell activation. Alternatively, AAVs may adsorb to cell surfaces and act as an activation signal itself. Current clinical trials exclude patients with pre-existing anti-AAV antibodies from enrolling; therefore, it is unlikely that ADCC will occur. The exact mechanism by which AAVs induce NK responses is still relatively unknown and requires further investigation.

Complement activation is another branch of innate immunity that is gaining traction in AAV activation of the adaptive immune response. Complement proteins circulate in blood and are activated by three distinct pathways: classical, lectin, and alternative, depending on the respective antigen. When activated by pathogens, complement will produce anaphylatoxins resulting in inflammation by mast cells and basophils, recruitment of immune cells and phagocytes, as well as formation of the membrane attack complex on infected cells resulting in their lysis. In the case of AAVs, AAV9 has been shown to initiate both the classical and alternative pathways leading to thrombotic microangiopathy in the clinic [26]. In vitro models showed involvement of only the classical pathway, triggered by anti-AAV-specific antibodies binding to the AAV capsid. This binding induces conformational changes in the C1q domain of the C1 complex, leading to the activation of C1r and C1s, which cleave C4 and C2 into their respective a and b subunits. This results in the formation of C3 convertase, which cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b. C3b contributes to the formation of C5 convertase, which then cleaves C5 into C5a and C5b, and forms the membrane attack complex, promoting lysis or enhanced phagocytosis. However, studies in non-human primates (NHPs) at a high dose of AAV suggest antibody-independent activation via the alternative pathway, initiated by spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 complex into C3(H2O) and amplified through C3bBb convertase [27]. Increased complement activation occurs in seropositive donor plasma incubated with AAV, and interestingly, complement proteins C1r, s, and q, C3b, CFH were shown to adsorb to the capsid surface [28]. C3b binds to complement receptor 1, which is present on B and T cells as well as monocytes and monocyte-derived dendritic cells (moDCs). Complement component adsorption to AAV particles could cause uptake into multiple immune cell types resulting in enhanced anti-AAV adaptive immunity. It is important to note that complement protein adsorption occurs to a very minor extent in seronegative donors [28].

Although we are gaining a more in-depth understanding of the interplay of innate factors and AAV, particularly the impact of pre-existing antibodies on complement activation, a clear case that demonstrates that much is still unknown is the death of a 27-year-old patient with advanced Duchenne muscular dystrophy after rAAV9-dSaCas9-VP64 administration [29]. This patient was given a high dose of 1×1014 VG/kg and died 8 days after treatment. The patient was also seronegative for anti-AAV9 and anti-Cas9 transgene antibodies or T-cell responses prior and post-administration [29]. An elevation of serum complement component SC5b-9 was observed 3 days after administration, as well as high interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, in a sample of pericardial fluid. Complement proteins C3 and C4 were also elevated on day 6. It is suggested that a high cytokine-mediated capillary leak syndrome developed, which led to acute respiratory distress syndrome and cardiac arrest 6 days after administration [29]. Because of the timing of cytokine generation, histological analysis, and the absence of adaptive immune mediators, this death has mainly been attributed to innate immune activation [29]. Of note, other patients who received the same dose of AAV9 did not have the same toxicity. Host factors and inherent properties of the vector could have led to unexpectedly high levels of the vector genome in the lung and heart, which may have contributed to the fatal outcome. Another case was a 16-year-old patient with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who died 6 days after AAV administration [30]. The patient had received a 2×1014 vg/kg dose and the death was attributed to innate immune response in the myocardium causing myocardial edema and heart failure. Although complement activation has been indicated in these patients, the cells responsible for large increases in cytokine production and downstream consequences have not been identified. One factor that has been identified to increase the risk of these toxicities is the dose of AAV. Severe toxicities have been observed in the highest dose cohorts in clinical AAV testing.

sec.title: Pre-Existing Immunity to AAV
sec.p: The overall pathway of generating an adaptive immune response to AAV is depicted in Fig. 2. Adeno-associated viral vectors were first isolated in 1965 by David Hoggan and Robert Atchison and thought to be a contaminant in cultures of simian and human adenoviruses [31, 32]. While AAVs alone are not able to replicate, hence being originally termed an “adenovirus-associated defective virus” by Atchinson, it was found that they gain this ability in the presence of a helper virus such as adenovirus or herpes. At these early times in AAV research, it was unknown that AAVs would pioneer gene therapy research, but even then, it was logical to assume that antibodies would form to virus-associated particles. Many AAV seroprevalence studies have been reported and a wide range of prevalence has been observed depending on the AAV serotype, geographic location, ethnic group, and age [33–35]. Generally, AAV1 and AAV2 have the highest seroprevalence of binding and neutralizing antibodies, which reach up to 72% of the population [35]. AAV7, AAV8, AAV5, and AAV9 range from 10 to 40% of the population [33, 34, 36]. Additionally, high cross-reactivity between serotypes has been observed [37]. Apart from the prevalence of anti-AAV antibodies in the population, there have also been reports of anti-AAV memory T cells in the blood of naturally infected humans [25, 38, 39].

sec.p: The major clinical implication of the widespread seroprevalence to AAVs has been the exclusion of seropositive individuals from trials or receiving approved therapies. Particularly for AAVs given intravenously or via a portal vein, it has been observed that even low titers of anti-AAV antibodies can prevent successful transduction or limit long-term efficacy of treatment [40, 41]. Apart from efficacy concerns, the ability of bound immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M to initiate the classical pathway of complement activation warrants safety concerns. For these reasons, alternative AAVs are being developed to evade antibodies to naturally occurring AAV while providing similar or increased transduction [42, 43]. Additionally, the route of administration plays a major role in the impact of anti-AAV pre-existing immunity on the efficacy of treatment. Particularly for immune privileged sites such as the eye, successful transduction was achieved after an intravitreal injection in patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with high anti-AAV antibody titers in sera [44]. The package insert for Luxturna, a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved AAV2-based gene therapy given by a subretinal injection, does not list the prevalence of pre-existing anti-AAV2 titers as a contraindication or exclusion criteria for receiving the therapy [45].

Administration of AAV to the central nervous system (CNS) or the brain has more conflicting evidence of the impact of pre-existing antibodies on the efficacy of treatment. Studies involving intraparenchymal delivery vary on assessment of serum anti-AAV antibodies prior to treatment. Higher thresholds of pre-existing antibodies have been set as exclusion criteria such as anti-AAV2 neutralizing titers >1:1200 prior to receiving therapy [46]. This is much higher than neutralizing titers shown to impact transduction in intravenously administered AAVs. Similarly, the package insert for Kebilidi, an AAV2 gene therapy given by intraputaminal infusion and recently granted accelerated approval by the FDA, does not list anti-AAV2 antibodies as a contraindication for receiving the therapy [47]. They state that the drug has only been tested on patients with < 1:1200 and the sample size was not large enough to determine if pre-existing titers had an impact on the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, safety, or efficacy of the drug [47]. Nevertheless, it has become accepted that there is less impact of pre-existing immunity on gene therapy success when given to immune-privileged sites such as the CNS, brain, or eye compared with routes that readily expose the antigen to circulating antibodies such as intravenous, intraportal, or intramuscular.

Multiple methods have been attempted to try to rid the influence of pre-existing antibodies on administration of AAVs. The use of empty capsid decoys prior to administration of genome-containing AAVs has been used with limited success [48]. IdeS, a bacterial endopeptidase approved for mismatched human leukocyte antigen (HLA) kidney transplants that cleaves Fc from (Fab)2, has been attempted to prevent neutralization for vector re-administration [49]. Additionally, plasmapheresis and immunoadsorption to specifically remove anti-AAV antibodies from patients’ blood before treatment has been attempted with limited success [50, 51]. While these methods lower the circulating anti-AAV antibodies, a near complete abolishment of Nab titers is needed for successful systemic administration of AAV vectors and is difficult to achieve.

sec.title: Humoral Response
sec.p: If patients are screened and determined to not have pre-existing immunity to the AAV serotype being given, the next immunological hurdle to overcome is de novo humoral and cellular immunity. De novo humoral immunity is characterized as the generation of an antibody response post-administration of AAV. These antibodies may target the capsid proteins of the AAV but also the transgene product as well. Nearly all patients treated systemically with AAV develop anti-AAV titers. This follows typical timelines for antibody development to therapeutic proteins with immunoglobulin M being produced ⁓1 week post-administration and production of high-affinity IgG antibodies ⁓ 2–3 weeks after administration [52]. Adeno-associated viral vectors distribute rapidly into tissues and are nearly absent from blood 48 hours after administration in NHPs [53]. In humans, concentrations of vector DNA in blood peaked between 1 and 9 days post-administration and encapsulated vector DNA was detectable in plasma 10 weeks after administration [54]. This is within the time window for anti-capsid immunoglobulin M to form and bind, which can cause antibody-dependent complement activation. The de novo generation of anti-AAV antibodies poses major limitations for re-dosing of patients if transgene production wanes. Given the high dose required for AAVs, a robust immune response occurs yielding higher titers than individuals with pre-existing immunity to natural infection. Subsequent administration of a different AAV serotype targeting the liver or muscle has been successful in rodent models [55, 56]. Similarly, in NHPs, hepatic gene delivery was achieved by sequential administration of AAV5ch and AAV1 [57]. This has not yet been attempted in humans. Similar methods to rid pre-existing anti-AAV antibodies described above have been attempted for AAV re-administration but have limited success because of the higher titers induced by initial AAV administration compared with natural infection [49].

Development of antibodies targeting the transgenic protein has been reported in NHPs [58]. The development of anti-transgene product antibodies will have a similar effect as an ADA response to therapeutic proteins. Development of neutralizing antibodies eliminates efficacy of the therapy, and binding antibodies can lead to other antibody-dependent potential toxicities (immune complex deposition, complement activation, ADCC). There is currently little clinical evidence for the emergence of anti-transgene product antibodies after AAV treatment, but this is because of the eligibility of patients receiving the therapies rather than the inherent tolerability of the transgene. For instance, in hemophilia A and hemophilia B clinical trials, patients were only allowed to enroll if they had already received >50 exposure days of recombinant Factor VIII or Factor IX, respectively [54, 59]. Fifty exposure days was not chosen arbitrarily, as it has been reported that patients receiving replacement therapy for this duration and have not developed antibodies being tolerized are at a low likelihood of developing titers in the future [60]. Therefore, when AAV is given expressing either as Factor VIII or Factor IX, individuals treated are at a very low propensity to form anti-transgenic protein antibodies. More data are needed in previously untreated patients to fully assess the risk of anti-transgenic protein antibody formation.

As the name “chimeric” implies, the introduced receptor in CAR T contains regions not of human origin, which can allow a patient to mount an anti-CAR T immunogenic response. This immune response can come in the form of a human anti-mouse antibody response as well as anti-CAR T cellular immunity, both of which have the potential to limit efficacy of the therapeutic [61]. Key determinants of CAR T success involve the kinetics of CAR T once they are administered to the patient. Typically, there are four phases of CAR T kinetics post-infusion, expansion, retraction, persistence, and elimination [62]. For the cells to have an adequate cancer-killing effect, a robust expansion phase must occur, allowing CAR T to proliferate rapidly as they engage with the cancer cells. Next, the cells retract and decline in circulating numbers as patient’s natural T-cell repertoire reestablishes. Finally, ideal CAR T persist in patients for long periods of time, killing the remaining cancer cells and preventing recurrence or secondary malignancies [63]. The presence of human anti-mouse antibodies (HAMAs) has the potential to bind the antigen-binding region of CAR, thereby neutralizing their therapeutic utility [64]. HAMAs may also bind other regions of CAR T with subsequent Fc binding to NK cells initiating ADCC, binding to DCs and macrophages, increasing clearance, or complement activation leading to complement-dependent cell lysis of CAR T. Importantly, the effect of HAMA responses varies significantly by the CAR design. Chimeric antigen receptors incorporating murine-derived single-chain variable fragment (scFv) regions such as FMC63-based anti-CD19 constructs are highly susceptible to anti-scFv antibody binding and neutralization as compared to humanized or fully human scFv versions. Clinical data from anti-CD19 CAR T therapies having murine scFv regions, such as Yescarta (CD28 based) and Kymriah (4-1BB based), indicate that although a small fraction of patients develop de novo anti-FMC63-binding antibodies, these antibodies generally did not affect initial expansion or early persistence of CAR T. This suggests that while humoral responses can be detected, their early impact on CAR T kinetics and efficacy may be limited by factors such as lymphodepletion and rapid CAR T expansion [65, 66]. Interestingly, for both Yescarta and Kymriah cell therapies, the presence of both pre-dose and post-dose antibodies did not impact the expansion or persistence of the cells [65, 66].

Beyond a humoral immune response, the source of the CAR T can also influence immune recognition and persistence. Chimeric antigen receptor T cells derived from patients’ own T cells (autologous) reduces the risk of immune rejection, whereas cells taken from healthy donors (allogeneic) are more susceptible to being recognized as foreign by the immune system [67]. Despite concerns about the rejection, allogeneic CAR T are often preferred in the clinic because of their rapid availability, consistent quality, and scalability. In the clinic, strategies such as lymphodepletion with chemotherapy along with alemtuzumab (anti-CD52 antibody) have been used to improve the short-term activity of allogeneic CAR T. CD52 was deleted from CAR T to avoid elimination by alemtuzumab [68], even though these allogeneic CAR T exhibited limited persistence after host T-cell recovery, underscoring the challenges posed by allo-reactive immunity [68]. Immune responses against CAR T are a major barrier in solid tumors. These responses often lead to rapid clearance and reduced efficacy [67]. Early murine-derived CARs frequently induced anti-CAR antibodies and HAMA responses, while even humanized or second-generation CARs can trigger humoral or cellular immunity, particularly without lymphodepletion [67]. Preconditioning regimens such as lymphodepletion have been shown to enhance CAR T expansion and persistence, and, in rare cases, achieve complete responses [67]. Minimizing immunogenicity through humanized constructs and preconditioning is therefore critical for improving therapeutic outcomes in patients with solid tumors. Humanized versions of CAR have been developed with increased efficacy compared to their chimeric counterparts, but a humoral response has still been observed [69].

sec.title: Cellular Response
sec.p: A cellular immune response to AAV manifests as an anti-capsid or anti-transgenic peptide cytotoxic T-cell response. As described in more depth in Sect. 1.1.1 of this review, TLR9 has been shown to be essential in the crosstalk between DCs to cross-present AAV capsid peptides via MHC I to develop a cytotoxic T-cell response in mice. Apart from this, transduced cells can present transgenic peptides in the context of MHC I as a signal for cytotoxic T-cell-mediated destruction. Destruction of transduced cells by cytotoxic T lymphocytes, whether targeting the AAV capsid or transgenic peptides, can lead to a loss of efficacy and toxicity in patients. Destruction of hepatic cells has led to elevations of liver transaminase activities posing safety concerns for liver-targeted gene therapies [22]. A cellular response to AAV capsid was observed in early AAV-mediated FIX gene therapy trials and peaked at 8–10 weeks post-infusion in two out of six individuals. This corresponded with a rise in liver transaminases and FIX transgene decline, signifying a high likelihood that AAV capsid peptides were being presented on hepatocytes up to 10 weeks after administration [41]. A single individual had detectable anti-capsid response in peripheral blood 33 weeks post-AAV administration [41]. This is evidence that administration of AAV can induce a durable cellular immune response in patients. The AAV administered in this study contained self-complementary DNA, which may have influenced the resulting immune profile.

Preclinical studies have demonstrated that excessive transgene expression following gene therapy can induce cellular stress and cytotoxicity, which may in turn trigger immune responses. Huichalaf et al. showed that overexpression of frataxin using an AAV9 vector in mice caused liver and heart toxicity, accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction and iron-sulfur cluster deficiency. This cellular stress can promote the release of damage-associated molecular patterns, which are recognized by innate immune cells and may amplify local inflammation [70]. Similarly, Suhy et al. reported that high levels of anti-HCV shRNA delivered via AAVs in NHPs induced hepatocellular toxicity, likely activating stress pathways in hepatocytes. The resulting cellular stress not only compromised tissue integrity but also had the potential to elicit immune activation against transduced cells [71]. In the CNS, T-cell infiltrates into the dorsal root ganglion have caused neurotoxicity in NHPs receiving CNS-targeting gene therapy, which was attributed to transgene overexpression in the dorsal root ganglia [72]. Although intravenous administration of AAVs can also deliver vectors to the CNS, such toxicity has not yet been observed in the clinic [73]. Importantly, only certain natural or engineered AAV capsids can cross the blood–brain barrier. AAV9, a naturally occurring capsid, can transduce the brain following intravenous delivery, though its efficiency is age dependent [74]. Engineered variants such as AAV-BBB6, AAAV-BBB28, and AAV-BBB31 (AAV1-like variant) have demonstrated an over 270-fold improvement in CNS transduction compared with AAV9, with a clear bias toward neuronal cells [75]. Together, these studies highlight that transgene overexpression can drive cytotoxicity-mediated immune responses, and they emphasize the need for careful dose optimization and promoter engineering to mitigate adverse immune effects while preserving therapeutic efficacy.

In an attempt to mitigate cellular and humoral immune responses to both the capsid and transgene product, intensive immunosuppressive regimens are typically given prior to and during treatment. These include the use of corticosteroids, sirolimus, rituximab, and others [76].

sec.title: Memory and Recall Response
sec.p: For both branches of adaptive immune response (humoral and cellular), a concern for subsequent dosing of AAV or CAR T is the presence of memory lymphocytes. Germinal centers formed by the initial encounter with antigens produce high affinity antibody-secreting plasma cells and long-lasting memory B cells that reside in lymph organs [77]. Memory B-cell receptors are primed for a specific antigen that upon subsequent exposure can rapidly proliferate and form ASCs to provide a robust antibody response towards the antigen [77]. Similarly, when T cells are initially primed with antigens, they may also form antigen-specific memory T cells that reside in lymph organs or peripheral tissues [78]. Adeno-associated viral vector seropositive individual PBMCs showed a distinct memory CD8+ response, B-cell differentiation into ASCs, and production of anti-capsid antibodies in vitro [25]. While peripheral memory and recall response can be monitored using ELISpot assays (IFN-γ for T cells, or IgG for B cells), flow cytometry, or the use of peptide tetramers, it is more difficult to assess tissue resident memory responses [79]. In the case of AAV, tissue resident CD8+ T cells pose a major concern that subsequent administration will cause rapid clearance of transduced cells and high levels of inflammation leading to increased toxicity [80]. Reinfusion of CAR T can present significant challenges owing to the limited persistence and reduced efficacy. In the case of CAR T, recall responses may target circulating CAR T, further hindering their persistence [64]. A recent study by Wang et al. analyzed patients with relapsed/refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma who failed the initial CD19/CD22 CAR T therapy and received a second infusion as salvage therapy along with other salvage treatments [81]. Although re-infusion produced higher short-term responses compared with other therapies, these were also accompanied by higher rates of severe infections, increased infection-related mortality, and low durability [81]. Persistence of CAR T is critical for long-term efficacy and the prevention of antigen-positive relapse in patients with cancer [82]. sec.title: Immunogenicity Prediction Methods for Gene and Cell Therapies
sec.p: Immunogenicity has been realized as a major hurdle to overcome in creating protein therapeutics such as monoclonal antibodies or replacement therapies. Immunogenicity in the form of anti-drug antibodies can have neutralizing potential rendering the drug non-efficacious but can also lead to safety concerns in terms of anti-drug antibody-drug complex deposition, leading to type III hypersensitivity reactions, complement activation, and phagocytic uptake [83]. For replacement therapies, cross-reactivity with an endogenous protein leading to an autoimmune state is a major safety concern [84]. Immunogenicity monitoring is required for the approval of new large-molecule drugs to clinical trials around the world as stated by the FDA, EMA, and others. Many of the lessons learned from the development of previously approved protein therapeutics can be adapted for use in novel AAV and cell-based therapies. sec.title: In Silico-Based Prediction Methods
sec.p: The first approach in assessing the immunogenic potential of the AAV or cell therapies is the use of in silico-based computer programs. Adeno-associated viral vectors are composed of proteins VP1, VP2, and VP3 consisting of 713–738 amino acids [85]. The chimeric antigen receptor in CAR T is also rather large, typically in the range of several hundred amino acids. Performing an epitope mapping in vitro analysis of such entities would be laborious and have high costs. To narrow down the scope of antigens required to test, in vitro programs have been developed that compare the sequence of the proposed construct or AAV to known HLA-binding epitopes. This makes use of databases such as IEDB (Immune Epitope Data Base), which is open source and routinely updated with novel epitopes, and the in vitro test used to identify them. Programs such as EpiMatrix developed by EpiVax utilize this information and a range of other data such as human proteomic data and known regulatory T-cell-inducing epitopes (Tregitopes) paired with modeling of input amino acid residues to fit within the binding pocket of HLA Class I and II molecules to rate individual peptides within a protein to be immunogenic or tolerogenic [86]. This analysis essentially breaks down the construct or protein of interest into individual 9-mer peptides, ranks each, and creates an overall score for the protein. It can even stratify by the most prevalent HLA subtypes and allows the user to compare the score with other known therapeutic antibodies and proteins with known immunogenicity [86]. This type of in silico analysis can be used during development to optimize the construct by protein engineering and aid in the selection of optimal replacement residues to be inserted into the protein. If a construct or AAV is going to be manipulated to rid contained epitopes, other testing must be conducted to verify that these changes do not alter critical aspects of the protein. Adeno-associated viral vector transduction potential should be confirmed, and for CAR T, target binding and activation must not be altered. Though an in silico assessment is a strong tool, it is typically not relied upon for final determination. It can be used to narrow drug candidates but ultimately the new drug product is then tested in vitro to ensure the desired properties are met [87].

One limitation of the current in silico programs is that they are limited to linear epitopes and currently do not predict conformational epitopes, therefore some epitopes may be overlooked. Additionally, these methods rely primarily on the HLA-T cell receptor interaction for prediction. While this is important, it ignores various other key factors that influence a product’s immunogenicity. Known factors such as aggregation or cellular impurities are not included in current in silico prediction algorithms, and in the case of AAV encapsulated genetic material or ability to bind immune-activating receptors such as TLRs will not be accounted for. Therefore, for confirmation and for screening of additional immune reactions that may occur, in vitro testing is still required.

sec.title: In Vitro Prediction Methods
sec.p: In vitro prediction methods utilize our working knowledge of how innate and adaptive immune responses are initiated in vivo. The general pathway of an antigen being phagocytosed by antigen-presenting cells, presented to naïve T cells to become effector cells, and downstream cell–cell interactions to create plasma cells producing antibodies toward the antigen is dissected. Most in vitro methods focus on the antigen-presenting cell–T-cell interaction as this primes the adaptive immune response, but screening additional factors such as innate stimulation and complement activation is possible.

sec.title: MHC-Associated Peptide Proteomics Assay (MAPPs)
sec.p: Multiple in vitro methods have been developed to enable epitope mapping and monitoring of the overall immunogenicity of therapeutic proteins, which can be applied to AAVs and CAR T therapies. The MAPPs (MHC-associated peptide proteomics) assay is one such assay, which consists of culturing human antigen-presenting cells with whole AAV, CAR T constructs, or peptide pools of each. Cells are allowed to uptake an antigen and mature, lysed, and HLA-peptide complexes are isolated via anti-HLA antibody-coupled microbeads [88, 89]. Post-isolation, peptides are eluted and then analyzed via high-performance liquid chromatography-mass Spectrometry [88, 89]. This method is powerful in its ability to predict epitopes but is highly labor intensive. Cells are typically cultured from PBMCs obtained from human donors and high sample numbers are required to adequately cover a wide range of HLA genotypes. Results from MAPPs assays can then be input into databases such as IEDB to further enhance future in silico analysis.

sec.title: Dendritic Cell (DC) Assays
sec.p: Dendritic cells are the initiators of the adaptive immune system as they capture the antigen, process it into peptides, and present it to T cells to propagate adaptive immunity. Dendritic cell assays are a powerful in vitro tool to test whether an adaptive immune response is likely to occur to a given therapeutic. Typically, DC assays involve culture of the DC in the presence of an antigen for activation and maturation, which is assessed by surface costimulatory molecules (CD40, CD80, CD86) and MHC presentation expression by flow cytometry and cytokines secreted (tumor necrosis factor-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-12) by an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay or Luminex assay. Dendritic cell assays have been implemented with the use of DCs obtained from non-human sources, derived from human PBMCs, and use of stable cell lines.

Murine DC cultures are cost effective and provide useful knowledge paired with in vivo studies in various disease models to gain a foundational understanding of DC interactions with antigens. Murine cells are typically taken for inbred rodents, which lack the genetic diversity of HLA types present in human donors. This allows for a culture method with less variability and increased standardization for immunogenicity screening. Murine bone marrow-derived DC cultures have been utilized for assessment of product-related factors for protein therapeutics such as the influence of aggregation on immunogenic outcomes and have now been applied to AAV immunogenicity to assess the immunogenic potential of empty capsids in AAV formulations [90, 91]. As murine DCs are not from a human origin, it is important to assess whether antigen recognition and processing reflects human DC processing. For instance, when assessing AAV immunogenicity in murine DC culture, the expression of proper TLRs and cytosolic sensors should be assessed to ensure similar activation pathways can be induced. Bone marrow-derived DCs mature in response to TLR2 and TLR9 ligands, making them beneficial in AAV immunogenicity assessment [92].

Both human and murine stable DC cell lines are available. JAWS II, a murine cell line, will have similar benefits as obtaining and culturing DCs directly from mice regarding low variability lot-to-lot, but will also have the same constraints of needing appropriate characterization to be able to translate to humans [93]. JAWS II cell lines were recently used to demonstrate that the inclusion of micro-RNA binding motifs on AAV1 capsids diminishes DC antigen presentation ability [94]. MUTZ-3 is a CD34+ human acute myeloid leukemia cell line that responds to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor and IL-4 to form DCs like the differentiation of monocytes into monocyte-derived DCs [95]. One limitation of MUTZ-3 cells is the poor TLR4 expression and signaling compared with moDCs [96, 97]. If it is anticipated that the therapeutic can potentially bind TLR4, this cell line will not be appropriate. Another cell line that has been used to test subunit vaccines in vitro is DC2.4, an immortalized murine DC line that has showed similar costimulatory molecule expression and cytokine secretion as human DCs [98]. While these may provide future benefit, industry currently relies primarily on human PBMC-derived DCs for an immunogenicity analysis.

Monocytes can be isolated from human PBMCs via negative selection by magnetic bead isolation. Monocytes cultured in the presence of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor and IL-4 form moDCs [99]. A benefit of these cells is that they incorporate the genetic diversity of HLA subtypes within the assay. Although this creates challenges to standardize the assay, with large enough sample numbers, a broad range of HLA subtypes can be assessed to provide a sensitive immunogenicity screening assay with clinical translatability [100]. Apart from assessing costimulatory molecule expression and cytokine secretion as metrics for moDC maturation, upregulation of chemokine receptor CXCR4 and migration towards chemokines CCL21 and CXCL12 correlate with clinical immunogenicity of therapeutic antibodies [101]. Considering immunogenic regions of CAR receptors are typically in the complementarity-determining regions of ScFv exposed on the surface of CAR T, and moDC migration captured the immunogenic potential of monoclonal antibody therapeutics that also have immunogenic complementarity-determining regions, there is high potential for this assay to be applied for immunogenicity screening of CAR constructs [102]. For AAV, moDC migration along with costimulatory molecule expression and cytokine secretion was also utilized to assess the impact of empty AAV capsids on AAV immunogenicity [90].

sec.title: DC–T-Cell Co-Culture Assays
sec.p: Dendritic cell–T cell coculture assays are powerful tools for immunogenicity screening. This method first requires stimulation of DCs with an antigen typically for 24–72 h, at which time the mature DCs are then cocultured with naïve CD4+ T cells for an additional 7–10 days. This design attempts to mimic interactions that typically occur in lymph nodes for priming an adaptive immune response. Cells are typically stained using carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester or CellTrace dyes to assess the proliferation of T cells [103, 104]. These dyes diffuse through cellular membranes and covalently bind amine residues on proteins within the cell. As the DCs interact with naïve T cells and in turn cause T-cell activation and proliferation, the dye is diluted and each successive generation of T cell can be monitored via changes in fluorescence intensity. Cytokine secretion from the T cells at the end of culture can be analyzed via an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay or Luminex assay for additional phenotyping and identification of the T helper-cell pathway induced by the antigen. Like DC assays, this method can be conducted using murine cells or human cells. When using human cells, DCs and T cells must be sourced from the same donor to ensure mismatched HLA does not interfere with the assay. The coculture of PBMC-derived moDCs with T cells isolated from the same individuals identified differences in T-cell responses to varying serotypes of AAV [105].

sec.title: Whole Blood and PBMC assays
sec.p: Whole blood and PBMC based assays are an attempt to take a less narrow focus when assaying immunogenicity in vitro. If the therapeutic is given systemically, then it naturally will come in contact with all components in the blood, therefore assessing immune response of cells in the blood space essentially simulates the early phase of immune activation in vivo. Whole blood from healthy donors and various cell subsets can then be isolated via flow-activated cell sorting or Ficoll gradient centrifugation. Whole blood or isolated cell subsets such as monocytes, lymphocytes, and granulocytes or PBMCs can then be challenged with an antigen. Supernatants of each challenge can then be analyzed for a panel of cytokines via Luminex to give an in-depth assessment of immune reactivity to antigen in the blood. This methodology was able to provide a sensitive method assessing immunogenic potential of antibody aggregates [100]. Incubation of AAV2 with PBMCs identified different activation pathways of seropositive and seronegative individuals’ responses and were the first data to implicate NK cell responses in AAV immunity [25]. Additionally, stimulation of PBMCs in seropositive donors allows for peptide mapping studies to identify immunodominant epitopes within the AAV capsid [106].

A primary use of PBMC stimulation assays has been to monitor for anti-AAV or anti-transgenic protein cellular immunity in patients or animals after receiving gene therapy. Interferon-γ enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISpot) assays of PBMCs have become the standard for a cellular immunogenicity assessment. These assays are commercially available and have been validated for use in an AAV setting [107]. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells are isolated from patient whole blood and stimulated with either AAV peptides or transgenic protein peptides on a PVDF membrane plate coated with an anti- IFN-γ capture antibody. As the cells are activated, they secrete IFN-γ that binds capture antibodies. A secondary anti-IFN-γ antibody conjugated to alkaline phosphatase is then added followed by BCIP/NBT to produce visual spots on the plate. Each spot is representative of a cell producing IFN-γ in response to the test antigen. These assays have been included in most AAV trials and have helped determine the influence of dose on an immunogenic response, the influence of immunosuppressive regimens on cellular immunity, as well as other factors contributing to AAV immunogenicity [58, 108, 109]. ELISpot assays have also been utilized to monitor anti-CAR cellular immune response in CAR T trials.

Current methods to monitor cellular immune responses to AAV or CAR T antigens in whole blood or cell subsets contained within monitor IFN-γ production by cells stimulated with a respective antigen. While ELISpot assays have been widely implemented, novel approaches are being developed to avoid drawbacks inherent in conducting ELISpot assays. Recently, a reverse transcriptase-droplet digital polymerase chain reaction analysis of IFN-γ gene expression was conducted to monitor antigen-specific cellular immune responses in whole blood and PBMCs of healthy donors previously vaccinated to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 [110]. This method was shown to have similar sensitivity to the ELISpot assay but required ten-fold fewer donor cells for analysis [110]. A droplet digital polymerase chain reaction provides advantages to traditional quantitative polymerase chain reaction approaches for gene quantification by eliminating the need of a standard curve to quantify data while providing a more sensitive, accurate, and reproducible result [111]. Droplet digital polymerase chain reaction has been utilized to monitor CAR T cellular kinetics in clinical studies [112]. The novel finding that it can accurately assess an antigen-specific cellular immune response may allow it to replace the need for IFN-γ ELISpot in the future. In addition to an IFN-γ analysis by reverse transcriptase-droplet digital polymerase chain reaction as a method to replace IFN-γ ELISpot, initial data have been generated for the qualification of a one-step whole blood-based method to monitor the cellular immune response to CAR T using TruCulture® tubes. The IFN-γ response to CEFX (peptide pool of known antigens) in PBMCs of healthy donors correlated with IFN-γ measured by the ELISpot assay. The TruCulture®-based method avoids the need for freeze-thawing patient cells, requires lower blood volumes, and is paired with cytokine multiplex assays to gain additional data and enhanced mechanistic insight into recall responses.

sec.title: Serum and Whole Blood-Based Complement Assays
sec.p: The emergence of thrombotic microangiopathy cases in gene therapy trials and the link of complement activation to thrombotic microangiopathy has sparked investigation into the factors contributing to AAV-mediated complement activation [26, 113]. The standard assay for assessing complement activity is determining a patient’s CH50, a metric of their plasma complement components ability to lyse sheep red blood cells pre-coated with rabbit anti-sheep antibodies [114]. Currently, in vitro methods to assess complement activation to AAV are rudimentary, in that serum from donors is typically incubated with AAV for 1 hour at 37 °C and then assessed for cleaved complement components via an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay [28]. Complement can be initiated by three separate pathways: classical, lectin, and alternative. The three pathways have different initiators but all three of these pathways converge to cleave complement components C3 and C5 into C3a/C3b and C5a/C5b, respectively. Hence, to assess AAV activation of any of the aforementioned pathways, these cleaved products are typically quantified in serum post-incubation with AAV. The classical pathway has been highly implicated in complement activation owing to this pathway being triggered at higher rates in seropositive donors.

Although it is well known that complement activation can lead to opsonization of antigen and subsequent uptake/clearance by antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and DCs, assessing factors of AAV that influence this pathway can be challenging. Smith et al. introduced AAV into the whole blood of seropositive and seronegative donors in the presence of a compstatin-based C3 and C3b inhibitor, APL-9 [115]. They observed that this inhibitor lowered CD86 levels on antigen-presenting cells, AAV uptake, and cytokine/chemokine secretion in response to AAV; therefore, demonstrating a link between complement activation and adaptive immune response induction [115]. Similarly, internalization of AAV2 by the human THP-1 monocyte cell line was enhanced in the presence of normal human plasma but not in heat-inactivated or C3-depleted plasma [116]. Multiple studies incubating AAV with serum have also demonstrated the ability of complement components to adsorb to AAV capsids, likely leading to these outcomes [28, 116].

sec.title: In Vivo Assessment of AAV Immunogenicity
sec.p: In vitro systems provide useful insight into screening immunogenicity of gene and cell therapies. They aim to recreate cellular interactions that occur in vivo to propagate immunity but the immune system is complex and many factors are overlooked when purely testing a therapeutic in vitro. The structure of lymphatics, non-immune cells that contribute to an immune response, distribution of drugs, and complex interactions such as the formation of germinal centers, require the use of in vivo models prior to administration in humans.

sec.title: Rodent Models for Immunogenicity Assessment
sec.p: Rodent models have been highly beneficial in the assessment of AAV immunogenicity and identifying factors that contribute to AAV immunogenicity. The use of KO mice, both total and conditional, has allowed for a more in-depth understanding of the influence of innate immunity on the induction of an adaptive immune response to AAV [17]. In addition to understanding pathways involved in AAV immunogenicity, in vivo murine studies have been utilized to assess product-related factors of AAV that contribute to immunogenicity such as the genetic material encapsulated (ssDNA vs single-cell DNA), serotype, or dose [108, 117, 118]. They also provide utility in the assessment of methods to circumvent pre-existing immunity [49]. Although meaningful data can be obtained in mouse studies, differences in immune response to AAV can be observed in humans. When assessing the immunogenicity of rhesus AAVrh.10 and AAV9, a much greater degree of cross-neutralization was observed in humans compared with mice [119]. Additionally, a major complication with mouse studies is the lack of cytotoxic activity of CD8+ T cells after AAV administration, which is observed in humans. Studies have shown anti-transgene CD8+ T cells do not proliferate and produce low levels of cytokines when challenged with antigens [120, 121]. Though generation of anti-AAV CD8+ T cells and memory T cells can be monitored, there is no evidence that they can lyse and clear vector-transduced hepatocytes in vivo in mouse models [122].

Various murine models have been utilized in the preclinical screening of CAR T therapies. Typically these models involve the use of immunodeficient strains of mice such as CB-17scid, non-obese diabetic-severe combined immunodeficiency, or non-obese diabetic/severe combined immunodeficiency/IL2Rγc-KO mice, which lack T and B cells, a complete adaptive immune response, or T and B and NK cells, respectively [123]. Immunodeficient mice are primarily used to prevent graft versus host rejection of human CAR T upon administration but add complications for monitoring anti-CAR immunogenicity because of the lack of adaptive immunity in these animals. Xenograft models have been developed that transplant either human tumor cell lines or primary patient-derived tumor cells to provide a target for CAR T, which is required to adequately monitor CAR T kinetics, efficacy, and toxicity [124, 125]. Xenograft models in humanized mice created by reconstitution of immune-depleted mouse strains with human immune and hematopoietic systems may provide the most useful tool in assessing anti-CAR T immunogenicity. While these mice will still have murine stromal cells, they will have human immune cells for CAR T to interact with and more accurately predict clinical consequences [123]. Murine studies using these models primarily focus on target binding and the cell-killing ability of CAR T as there are few data on anti-CAR immunogenicity in mouse models.

sec.title: Primate Models for Immunogenicity Assessment
sec.p: Non-human primates are often used in preclinical drug development to determine first-in-human dosing as well as toxicology evaluations because of the similarity in anatomy and biological function as humans. With immunogenicity being a concern for gene and cell therapies, they are highly utilized to screen for factors that influence AAV immunogenicity when developing novel vectors. Often factors identified in mice are corroborated in NHPs to ideally enhance the translatability of results. Factors such as the choice of immunosuppressive regimen given upon administration of AAV, AAV serotype, route of administration, or the impact of pre-existing antibodies or de novo generated antibodies on AAV gene therapy [126–130]. Non-human primates are naturally infected with AAVs, which makes them an ideal model for testing approaches to mitigate pre-existing immunity to AAV [51, 131]. Recently, it was shown that the primate MHC haplotype (Mamu-A002.01) was associated with cardiac toxicity related to the GAA transgene [132]. Furthermore, an immunodominant peptide within the transgene was confirmed via ELISpot epitope mapping [132]. With results such as this, the sponsors can then either alter the transgene construct or run an in silico and in vitro analysis to predict whether this epitope is likely to bind to human HLA and produce a similar reaction in humans.

Toxicity is a major concern for AAVs entering the clinic. Like humans, high doses of systemic AAV have been shown to cause rises in liver transaminases, complement activation, and liver injury in NHPs [133]. High systemic doses of AAV have also been shown to cause dorsal root ganglion degeneration, which may be linked to inflammation and immune response generated to the vector, and has raised a concern for future CNS-targeted AAVs [134]. Non-human primates currently play an essential role in the development of novel vectors to optimize the vectors and prevent immune-related toxicities in the clinic. Primate studies are cumbersome, expensive, and provoke ethical concerns, but their utility is unmatched for screening novel vectors prior to human use. For these reasons, they are only conducted when deemed essential and supportive data for a therapy cannot be provided by other means.

The use of NHPs has also been influential in the development of CAR T therapies. Certain primate cancers contain CAR T targets that are highly homologous to human cancers and similar expression patterns such as receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor 1 (ROR1) expressed in B-cell malignancies [135]. In this study, they showed that a T-cell immune response occurred >3–4 weeks that coincided with the elimination of CAR T in all animals, which prevented the study from establishing long-term safety of the therapy. Like murine studies of CAR T, primate studies typically focus on determining efficacy of the therapy and addressing toxicity concerns driven by the potent activation of CAR T engaging with cancer. Toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, which pose a major issue in the clinic have been studied in NHPs [136]. A challenge for studying anti-CAR immunogenicity in primates is like that of murine models. Primates typically receive intensive immunodepleting therapies prior to administration of CAR T to prevent graft versus host rejection of therapy. This in turn can prevent the generation of anti-CAR immunogenicity. Nevertheless, as mentioned above, it is possible to monitor anti-CAR immunity in NHPs. Typically, anti-CAR immunogenicity is not included in the study design of a NHP preclinical assessment as their primary focus is related to toxicity of treatment driven by overactivation of the therapeutic. Including anti-CAR immunogenicity endpoints will allow for a greater understanding of anti-CAR immunogenicity and development of less immunogenic CAR T.

sec.title: Capsid Modification
sec.p: Capsid engineering has been used to actively reduce AAV immunogenicity by altering the surface-exposed capsid region to avoid immune recognition. For instance, mutating surface tyrosine in an AAV2 capsid to phenylalanine reduces phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation, thereby lowering MHC I antigen presentation and T-cell-mediated clearance. This mutant is highly efficient in transducing a variety of cells and tissues and is efficacious in phase I and II clinical trials with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Additionally, genetic modification of the VP1 and VP2 region was also explored. A single-chain antibody targeting CD34 was fused to the N-terminus of VP1, VP2, and VP3 region of the AAV2 capsid. This strategy showed extremely low titers for the modified capsid as compared with the wild-type capsid [137]. However, not all approaches have succeeded: strategies that removed or masked known epitopes sometimes exposed novel immunogenic regions, leading to new T-cell responses that offset the intended benefit. For instance, structure-guided mutation of a neutralizing epitope in AAV9 (targeting the monoclonal antibody PAV9.1) did reduce its binding, but did not improve evasion of polyclonal neutralizing sera, likely because other antigenic regions remained exposed [138]. Thus, while some capsid modifications excel in reducing immune activation in preclinical models, translation to clinical settings remains challenging.

sec.title: Conclusions and Future Directions
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell and AAV gene therapies are hampered by various immunogenic concerns. Preclinical methods described above have allowed sufficient assessment of gene and cell therapy immunogenicity for multiple products to make it to market and treat patients with life-threatening and debilitating diseases. Further investigation of mechanisms driving immunity toward each therapy will help develop novel screening tools with increased translatability. As more data accumulate of immunogenic epitopes observed in in vitro assays and are input into public databases, better informed in silico predictions will be made. The recent passing of the FDA Modernization Act 2.0, which allows drugs to be approved without the use of animal models, has given an additional push to industry to develop novel in vitro methods to avoid the need of animal studies [139]. Although this is promising, to date there has not been an approved gene or cell therapy that was not first tested in animals.

Some novel methods that are being developed that may provide utility in future immunogenicity assessments is the use of three-dimensional organoids, organ-on-a-chip devices, or even body-on-a-chip devices [140]. These systems layer multiple cell types and can provide fluid flow and mechanical stress to create in vitro systems that more accurately resemble human anatomy. While only a few studies have been implemented for the use of AAVs or CAR T in these systems, they have great potential to revolutionize in vitro screening. For instance, lymphoid follicles were able to be produced in an organ-on-a-chip setting, which were capable of plasma cell differentiation and antibody production to influenza as well as cytokine response on clinically relevant time scales [141]. The formation of germinal centers and IgG production is a major feature of adaptive immunity, which has required in vivo experimentation until now.

Many AAVs are currently in clinical trials and some AAV and CAR T therapies have already been approved. As the field continues to grow, we continue to realize new immunological challenges that need to be accounted for. An adeno-associated viral vector and CAR T preclinical immunogenicity assessment is adjusting to accommodate these occurrences. For instance, with the recent realization that complement activation can lead to severe toxicity in individuals treated with AAVs, there has been increased investigation and development of assays to assess factors contributing to AAV-mediated complement activation. In terms of CAR T therapy, emerging reports highlight a rare but important safety concern: the development of secondary malignancies. In 2023–4, the FDA issued safety communications following case reports of CAR T-associated T-cell lymphomas [142, 143]. The proposed mechanisms include vector-mediated insertional mutagenesis, where retroviral or lentiviral integration near proto-oncogenes may drive clonal expansion, and chronic immune activation, where prolonged antigen stimulation and inflammatory cytokine exposure impose selective pressure on engineered T cells, potentially favoring the outgrowth of abnormal or transformed clones. Anti-CAR T immunogenicity may contribute to this phenomenon by targeting CAR T, where resistant clones with proliferative or oncogenic advantages dominate. Thus, the FDA now states that CAR T recipients should be monitored life-long for new malignancies [142]. In terms of preclinical screening assays, there is no one-size-fits-all approach for predicting immunogenicity of gene and cell therapies. Rather, multiple assays should be utilized, which rely on our mechanistic understanding of immune activation. Ideally, our preclinical assessment aids in the production of therapies with better efficacy and safety profiles and forewarns about possible toxicity issues that may arise in the clinic.
